summary:
Humans have left machines, memorials and even a family photograph across two worlds. This project imagines a ring of caretaker bases that would listen for them, clean their panels and carry their data home.
Fifty years of spacecraft and keepsakes now sit silently on the Moon and Mars. Abandoned but Not Forgotten maps the small bases that could keep them company, and the stories behind each one. Every mission to the Moon and Mars left machines behind. This project proposes bases that would keep in touch with them.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?
The page is a single self-contained HTML file. A 3D globe, drawn on a canvas, shows every abandoned object as a dot and every proposed base as a diamond. Dashed lines connect each base to the equipment it would serve. Selecting a base turns the globe to it and opens a record with its story, its reasons for being chosen, and the objects in its care. A ledger lists the same objects by age, and a reference list ties each claim to a source. Nothing is fetched at runtime, so the page works offline once loaded.

What benefits does it have?

  • It collects scattered, hard-to-find facts about dozens of missions in one place, each with a source.
  • It treats old hardware as something worth maintaining, not only as debris.
  • It puts the protection of historic sites, such as the Apollo landing areas, into the same picture as science and reuse.
  • It is easy to browse: a visitor can learn the whole story from the globe alone, or dig into the sources.

What is the intended impact of the project?
The aim is to start a conversation about what happens to hardware and heritage on other worlds as crewed missions return. Concretely, it could help mission planners weigh whether to recover, relay with, or protect existing equipment, support preservation of the Apollo sites, and encourage reuse projects such as NASA’s LunaRecycle Challenge. For the public, it makes that history visible and memorable.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript (no framework or build step).
  • Graphics: The HTML canvas API for the globe, with a pixel-level projection and a schematic texture generated in code.
  • Fonts: Google Fonts (Jost and Newsreader).
  • Hosting and sharing: A Claude artifact link.
  • Research: Web search for mission records and published research, with the sources listed on the page.
  • Hardware: Laptop, Tablet, Phone.

How is your project creative?

  • It frames mission debris as heritage, asking people to care for objects they usually treat as garbage.
  • The globe is the main interface, with the abandoned objects and proposed bases placed where they are on the real surface.
  • Each object is told as a short story (the golf balls, the family photo, the Apollo 17 rover parked to film its own launch), so the facts feel human.
  • The two-world design gives the Moon and Mars their own visual identities.
  • A ticking timer makes the length of abandonment feel immediate.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Accuracy: Every object and base is tied to a reference, and the page marks the base sites as its own proposal.
  • Respect for historic sites: The Apollo locations are protected by the One Small Step Act, so the proposal keeps bases away from them.
  • Access: The page supports keyboard navigation, reduced-motion settings, dark and light palettes, and a text-only view of the data through the ledger.
  • Practicality: Base sites were chosen for landing ground, nearby ice or shelter where it exists, and distance to the equipment they would serve.

Every mission to the Moon and Mars has left something behind: landers that went dark, rovers that drove until they couldn’t, probes crashed on purpose, and a few personal keepsakes such as a family photograph, two golf balls and a small aluminum astronaut honoring the fallen. None of it was ever meant to come home. Abandoned but Not Forgotten maps all of it and proposes a network of caretaker bases that would go back to these machines. The bases would clean their panels, fit new beacons, collect what they recorded and keep listening for anything that can still answer.

You spin a 3D globe of the Moon or Mars, choose a base and follow the glowing links to the old equipment it would look after. Each object has its own story: how it arrived, what it found, how it went silent, and what a caretaker crew could do for it now.

Features

  • Two worlds, one switch: Move between a starlit Moon in gold and black and a rust-red Mars under a butterscotch sky.
  • 20 objects left behind: These range from Surveyor 1 and Tranquility Base to Spirit, Opportunity, InSight and the Ingenuity helicopter.
  • 13 proposed bases: Each site was chosen for a reason, such as lava-tube shelter, buried ice, safe landing ground or a short drive to history.
  • A live clock of silence: One counter ticks every second, and a ledger shows how long each object has waited alone.
  • The bigger question: Should we protect these sites, study them, reuse them, or reconnect with them? The project argues for reconnecting.
  • Fully sourced: It has 46 numbered references from NASA, JPL, peer-reviewed journals and U.S. law.
